blocks.text: Imagine trying to solve a puzzle, but every time you think you have a solution, the rules change. This is what happens when we deal with undecidable problems in computability.

blocks.markdown: In computability theory, reductions are a powerful tool used to demonstrate the undecidability of problems. A reduction is a way of transforming one problem into another, such that a solution to the second problem would provide a solution to the first. This concept is crucial in proving that certain problems cannot be solved by any algorithm.

blocks.title: Reduction
blocks.text: A reduction from problem A to problem B is a method of solving A using a solution to B. If B is undecidable, then A must also be undecidable.

blocks.markdown: The classic example of an undecidable problem is the Halting Problem. The Halting Problem asks whether a given program will eventually stop running or continue to run forever. Alan Turing proved that there is no algorithm that can solve the Halting Problem for all possible program-input pairs.

blocks.latex: HALT = \{ (P, x) \mid \text{program } P \text{ halts on input } x \}
blocks.caption: The set HALT represents the Halting Problem.

blocks.markdown: To prove that another problem is undecidable, we can use a reduction from the Halting Problem. If we can transform instances of the Halting Problem into instances of another problem in such a way that solving the new problem would solve the Halting Problem, then the new problem must also be undecidable.

blocks.title: Reduction from the Halting Problem
blocks.prompt: Prove that the problem of determining whether a Turing machine accepts a given input is undecidable.

steps.text: Define the problem L as the set of pairs (M, w) where M is a Turing machine and w is an input string that M accepts.
Assume there exists a decider D for L. We will use D to decide the Halting Problem, leading to a contradiction.
Construct a Turing machine M' that simulates M on w and halts if M accepts w.
Use D to determine if M' accepts w. If D says yes, then M halts on w; otherwise, it does not.
Since deciding the Halting Problem is impossible, our assumption that D exists must be false. Thus, L is undecidable.

blocks.answer: The problem of determining whether a Turing machine accepts a given input is undecidable.

blocks.title: Direction of Reduction
blocks.text: To prove a problem is undecidable, reduce from a known undecidable problem to the problem in question.

blocks.markdown: Let's consider another example. Suppose we want to prove that the problem of determining whether a Turing machine enters a specific state is undecidable. We can use a reduction from the Halting Problem.

blocks.title: Reduction to State Problem
blocks.prompt: Prove that the problem of determining whether a Turing machine enters a specific state is undecidable.

steps.text: Define the problem S as the set of triples (M, w, q) where M is a Turing machine, w is an input string, and q is a state that M enters when processing w.
Assume there exists a decider D for S. We will use D to decide the Halting Problem, leading to a contradiction.
Construct a Turing machine M' that enters state q if and only if M halts on input w.
Use D to determine if M' enters state q. If D says yes, then M halts on w; otherwise, it does not.
Since deciding the Halting Problem is impossible, our assumption that D exists must be false. Thus, S is undecidable.

blocks.answer: The problem of determining whether a Turing machine enters a specific state is undecidable.

points: Reductions transfer undecidability from one problem to another.
To prove undecidability, reduce from a known undecidable problem.
The direction of reduction is crucial: from the known to the unknown.
